strengths: Rigorously extends theoretical framework to modern LLM architectures (Gemma, Llama, Falcon, MoE) that were not covered by prior work, addressing specific gaps for bias-free and gated architectures with RMSNorm

Introduces elegant unified 'controllability' framework (input/output controllability) that provides conceptually clean lens for understanding diverse architectural patterns and proves impossibility results for certain designs
Provides constructive proofs with clear separation of concerns: rank-1 updates correct input changes while output updates absorb residual differences, with valid mathematical derivations throughout

Validates theory on real models (Gemma 3 1B/4B, Falcon 7B) with comprehensive experiments showing 100% token-level match in float32 and near-perfect logit distributions, including multi-modal (image) contexts
Comprehensive treatment with rigorous appendices including formal proofs, numerical stability analysis (RMSNorm inversion with Lagrange multipliers), impossibility theorems, and extensive ablations
weaknesses: Critical gap between theory and practice: claims of 'perfect equivalence' are undermined by substantial numerical stability issues—bfloat16 performance degrades to 87.5% token match without mitigation, and 'stable' update uses L2-minimizing approximation rather than exact solution, yet this is relegated to Appendix B rather than main narrative

Severely limited practical applicability: token-dependent patches require recomputation at each generation step (computationally prohibitive for inference), only provides single-token equivalence, and multi-token generation breaks due to attention values on newly generated tokens, making the framework primarily descriptive rather than prescriptive

Incremental theoretical contribution: core insight (context→weight patches) originates from Dherin et al. (2025); extension to modern architectures is natural engineering work but lacks significant conceptual novelty beyond architectural accommodation

Experimental validation has notable limitations: only 5-6 prompt examples with 'Mars forecast' dominant, restricted to smaller models (1B-7B), no computational cost analysis or comparison to alternative ICL explanation methods, and multi-modal validation (Figure 5) is superficial without theoretical grounding

Architectural brittleness: Theorem 3 requires output-controllability which fails for certain configurations (proven in Theorem 4); real models happen to satisfy this but framework feels contingent rather than principled, limiting applicability to future architectures

Numerical precision requirements inadequately addressed in main text: element-wise division in Eq. (4) has no safeguards, RMSNorm inversion requires careful implementation, and the stable update introduces additional approximation error that undermines 'perfect' equivalence claims

strengths: Technically sound mathematical proofs extending implicit weight patch theory from vanilla to modern transformer architectures
Elegant general framework based on input/output controllability that abstracts across diverse architectures (Gemma, Llama, Falcon, MoE)
Practical algorithm (Algorithm 1) with numerical stabilization considerations for multi-layer models
Comprehensive coverage of modern architectural components (gating, RMSNorm, bias-free designs, pre/post-norm)
Honest discussion of limitations including architectural prerequisites and assumptions
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily an engineering extension of Dherin et al. (2025); core insight of rank-1 patches via input/output controllability decomposition is not new

Token-dependent equivalence is fundamentally limiting: updates must be recomputed per token, so mechanism does not explain how ICL works during actual inference with frozen weights; this directly undermines claims about understanding in-context learning

Numerical stability issues undermine 'perfect equivalence' claims: division by small values causes bfloat16 performance to drop to 87.5% token matching; complex RMSNorm inversion required; claims of 'perfect match' are misleading when precision matters

Experimental validation limited to small models (1-7B parameters), simple generation tasks with argmax decoding, and relatively short sequences; unclear if approach scales or numerical issues worsen with larger models and longer contexts

No demonstration of practical applications: paper validates theory but provides no evidence that understanding this mechanism enables useful capabilities (efficiency improvements, better architecture design, improved fine-tuning, etc.)

Architectural constraints presented as facts rather than analyzed for design implications: Theorem 4 proves controllability fails for certain architectures, but implications for future design are not discussed
Per-token divergence: experimental setup forces updated model to follow baseline tokens when they diverge, making it artificial to assess whether updates truly preserve behavior in free generation

Important content relegated to appendices (22 pages total): numerical stabilization details, RMSNorm inversion derivation, gradient descent connection, and experimental ablations should be better integrated into main narrative

strengths: Rigorous mathematical framework extending implicit weight patch theory to modern LLM architectures (Gemma, Llama, Falcon, etc.) with careful proofs of Theorems 1-3
Addresses real gaps in prior work (Dherin et al. 2025): biases, gating mechanisms, RMSNorm, and post-normalization schemes systematically handled
Elegant unifying framework based on input/output controllability (Definitions 1-2, Theorem 3) that could be valuable for analyzing future architectures
Sophisticated treatment of numerical stability with analytical RMSNorm inversion (Appendix B) achieving 100% float32 and 87.5→100% bfloat16 token matching with stabilization
Impossibility results (Theorem 4) proving fundamental limits for certain architectures, demonstrating theoretical depth
Comprehensive appendices with gradient interpretation, ablations on layer depth, and extended experimental results
weaknesses: Significant gap between theoretical claims of perfect equivalence and practical achievability: requires approximate RMSNorm inversion and achieves only 87.5% token match in bfloat16 without stabilization

Token-dependent patches must be recomputed for each generation step, severely limiting practical utility; the paper acknowledges this as a limitation but provides no solution, instead referencing concurrent work (Mazzawi et al. 2025)
Insufficient exploration of failure modes: Theorem 1 condition f(·)ᵢ ≠ 0 is stated but not analyzed; workaround of dividing by 1 to avoid NaN is ad-hoc; no quantitative analysis of failure frequency

Limited experimental validation: only 5 prompts with constrained diversity, two model architectures, and no ablations on context length/complexity; experiments primarily verify theory works rather than exploring failure modes

Incremental contribution over Dherin et al. (2025): core insight (context→weight patches) is prior work; extension to modern architectures while non-trivial is somewhat expected; no novel inference algorithms or architectural insights emerge
Error accumulation across layers not formally analyzed: Algorithm 1 uses outputs with patches applied, claiming to be 'self-correcting' but lacking theoretical error bounds
Limited exploration of implications: no mechanistic interpretability insights, no architectural design recommendations; unclear why practitioners should care beyond theoretical interest
Missing discussion of attention layer dynamics: A(C,x) treated as black box; all analysis focuses on how MLPs absorb residual differences
